# Consumption (tuberculosis) is contagious (`tuberculosis_control`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, microscope, pasteurisation, xrays
- Core idea: Consumption, the slow wasting cough that killed about one adult in five in European cities around 1800, is neither inherited nor a matter of temperament. It is caught by breathing what the sick cough out, mostly over months in crowded, closed, dark rooms, and children catch a form in glands and bones from the milk of sick cows. So: the cougher sleeps alone, coughs into a cloth that is boiled and spits into a pot that is emptied into the fire; rooms are aired and sunned; milk is boiled; nobody with a long cough nurses children or handles food. Rest and good food help the body hold the disease but cure nothing; real cures came with streptomycin and later drugs, taken for many months.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calling it hereditary because it runs in households; that is contagion among people who share a room
  - Romantic ideas of consumption as a disease of sensitive souls; the royal touch for scrofula
  - Believing raw milk is healthier; bovine tuberculosis was a major killer of children
  - Promising a cure: mountain air, sanatoria and Koch's tuberculin (1890) did not cure
  - Stopping treatment when the patient feels better, which breeds resistant disease
- History: egypt: c. 3000–1000 BC – spinal tuberculosis in mummies; americas: c. AD 1000 – tuberculosis in Peruvian mummies, long before European contact; 1943–1944 streptomycin reported by Schatz, Bugie and Waksman at Rutgers; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's Canon treats phthisis as contagious; europe: 1546 – Fracastoro lists phthisis among contagions; 1699 Lucca and 1782 Naples order reporting and disinfection; 1865 Villemin transmits it to rabbits; 1882 Koch finds the bacillus; 1921 BCG vaccine (Calmette and Guérin); 1948 British streptomycin trial, a landmark randomised trial with concealed allocation
- Read:
  - Robert Koch, Die Aetiologie der Tuberculose, Berliner klinische Wochenschrift (1882)
  - Thomas Dormandy, The White Death: A History of Tuberculosis (1999)
  - Helen Bynum, Spitting Blood: The History of Tuberculosis (2012)
